questions.q: What real milestone in the course does this lesson mark, per the instructor?
options: Moving from individual Solidity concepts to actually building real-world applications
The very first lesson of the entire course
The end of the course, right before the final exam
A return to reviewing only basic syntax
questions.explain: The instructor stated directly that the class had covered most basic Solidity concepts and was now moving on to real-world applications, starting with this Ether wallet.

questions.q: What does the EtherWallet contract's real goal state?
options: Anyone can send ETH; only the owner can withdraw
Only the owner can send ETH; anyone can withdraw
Nobody can send or withdraw ETH
Only registered voters can interact with the contract
questions.explain: The contract's own comments state its exact purpose: anyone can send ETH into it, but only the owner can withdraw it back out.

questions.q: Why does the contract need a dedicated `receive() external payable {}` function?
options: It's the special function that lets the contract accept plain Ether transfers with no function call attached
It's required for every Solidity contract, even ones that never handle Ether
It replaces the need for a constructor
It performs the withdrawal logic
questions.explain: receive() is Solidity's special mechanism for accepting plain ETH sent directly to the contract's address, without calling any specific function.

questions.q: Why must `owner` be declared as `address payable` instead of a plain `address`?
options: Solidity only allows calling .transfer() on an address payable, not a plain address
Plain addresses can't be stored in a contract at all
It's purely a style convention with no functional effect
address payable is required for every state variable regardless of type
questions.explain: Since withdraw() calls .transfer() on owner, owner must be an address payable — Solidity's compiler enforces this distinction directly.

questions.q: What real check inside `withdraw` actually enforces "only the owner can withdraw"?
options: require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not owner")
A check on the amount being withdrawn
The receive() function
The pragma statement
questions.explain: This require statement compares the caller's address to the stored owner address, reverting the transaction for anyone else.
